Norovirus
Norovirus, also known as Norwalk virus, is the most common cause of <color=#3366CC>gastroenteritis</color>. The infection, sometimes
referred to as the winter vomiting disease, is characterized by non-bloody <color=#3366CC>diarrhea</color>, <color=#3366CC>vomiting</color>, and <color=#3366CC>stomach pain</color>. Fever
or headaches may also occur. Symptoms usually develop 24 hours after being exposed, and recovery typically occurs
within one to three days. Complications are uncommon, but may include <color=#3366CC>dehydration</color>, especially in the young, the old,
and those with other health problems.
The <color=#3366CC>virus</color> is usually spread by the <color=#3366CC>fecal–oral route</color>. This may be through contaminated food or water or
person-to-person contact. It may also spread via contaminated surfaces or through <color=#3366CC>air</color> from the vomit of an infected
person. Risk factors include unsanitary food preparation and sharing close quarters. Diagnosis is generally based on
symptoms. Confirmatory testing is not usually available but may be performed by public health agencies during
outbreaks.
Prevention involves proper <color=#3366CC>hand washing</color> and disinfection of contaminated surfaces. There is no <color=#3366CC>vaccine</color> or specific
treatment for norovirus. Management involves <color=#3366CC>supportive care</color> such as drinking sufficient fluids or <color=#3366CC>intravenous fluids</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Oral rehydration solutions</color> are the preferred fluids to drink, although other drinks without <color=#3366CC>caffeine</color> or <color=#3366CC>alcohol</color> can help.
<color=#3366CC>Hand sanitizers</color> based on <color=#3366CC>alcohols</color> tend to be ineffective against noroviruses due to their being non-enveloped,
although some virus genotypes are more susceptible.
Norovirus results in about 685 million cases of disease and 200,000 deaths globally a year. It is common both in the
<color=#3366CC>developed</color> and <color=#3366CC>developing world</color>. Those under the age of five are most often affected, and in this group it results in
about 50,000 deaths in the developing world. Norovirus infections occur more commonly during winter months. It often
occurs in outbreaks, especially among those living in close quarters. In the United States, it is the cause of about half of
all <color=#3366CC>foodborne disease</color> outbreaks. The virus is named after the city of Norwalk, Ohio, where an outbreak occurred in
Signs and symptoms
Norovirus infection is characterized by <color=#3366CC>nausea</color>, <color=#3366CC>vomiting</color>, watery <color=#3366CC>diarrhea</color>, abdominal pain, and in some cases, loss of
taste. A person usually develops symptoms of <color=#3366CC>gastroenteritis</color> 24 hours after being exposed to norovirus. General
lethargy, weakness, muscle aches, headaches, and low-grade fevers may occur. The disease is usually self-limiting,
and severe illness is rare. Although having norovirus can be unpleasant, it is not usually dangerous, and most who
contract it make a full recovery within two to three days.
Norovirus can establish a long-term infection in people who are <color=#3366CC>immunocompromised</color>, such as those with common
variable immunodeficiency or with a suppressed immune system after <color=#3366CC>organ transplantation</color>. These infections can be
with or without symptoms. In severe cases, persistent infections can lead to norovirusassociated enteropathy, intestinal
villous <color=#3366CC>atrophy</color>, and malabsorption.
Virology
Transmission
Noroviruses are transmitted directly from person to person (62–84% of all reported outbreaks) and indirectly via
contaminated water and food. Transmission can be aerosolized when those stricken with the illness vomit or by a toilet
flush when vomit or diarrhea is present; infection can follow eating food or breathing air near an episode of vomiting,
even if cleaned up. The viruses continue to be shed after symptoms have subsided, and shedding can still be detected
many weeks after infection.
Vomiting, in particular, transmits infection effectively and appears to allow <color=#3366CC>airborne transmission</color>. In one incident, a
person who vomited spread the infection across a restaurant, suggesting that many unexplained cases of food
poisoning may have their source in vomit. In December 1998, 126 people were dining at six tables; one person vomited
onto the floor. Staff quickly cleaned up, and people continued eating. Three days later, others started falling ill; 52
people reported a range of symptoms, from fever and nausea to vomiting and diarrhea. The cause was not immediately
identified. Researchers plotted the seating arrangement: more than 90% of the people at the same table as the sick
person later reported becoming ill. There was a direct correlation between the risk of infection of people at other tables
and how close they were to the sick person. More than 70% of the diners at an adjacent table fell ill; at a table on the
other side of the restaurant, the infection rate was still 25%. The outbreak was attributed to a Norwalk-like virus
(norovirus). Other cases of transmission by vomit were later identified.
In one outbreak at an international scout jamboree in the Netherlands, each person with gastroenteritis infected an
average of 14 people before increased hygiene measures were put in place. Even after these new measures were
enacted, an ill person still infected an average of 2.1 other people. A US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
(CDC) study of 11 outbreaks in New York State lists the suspected <color=#3366CC>mode of transmission</color> as person-to-person in seven
outbreaks, foodborne in two, waterborne in one, and one unknown. The source of waterborne outbreaks may include
water from municipal supplies, wells, recreational lakes, swimming pools, and ice machines.
<color=#3366CC>Shellfish</color> and salad ingredients are the foods most often implicated in norovirus outbreaks. Ingestion of shellfish that
has not been sufficiently heated – under 75 C – poses a high risk for norovirus infection. Foods other than shellfish may
be contaminated by infected food handlers. Many norovirus outbreaks have been traced to food that was handled by
only one infected person.
From March to August 2017, in Quebec, Canada, there was an outbreak of norovirus that sickened more than 700
people. According to an investigation by Canada's CFIA Food Control Agency, the culprit was frozen raspberries
imported from Harbin Gaotai Food Co Ltd, a Chinese supplier. Canadian authorities subsequently issued a recall on
raspberry products from Harbin Gaotai.
According to the CDC, there was a surge in norovirus cases on thirteen <color=#3366CC>cruise ships</color> in 2023, which marks the highest
number of outbreaks since 2012.
Classification
Noroviruses (NoV) are a genetically diverse group of single-stranded positive-sense RNA, non-enveloped viruses
belonging to the family Caliciviridae. According to the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses, the genus
Norovirus has one species: Norwalk virus (Norovirus norwalkense).
Noroviruses can genetically be classified into at least seven different genogroups (GI, GII, GIII, GIV, GV, GVI, and
GVII), which can be further divided into other genetic clusters or <color=#3366CC>genotypes</color>.
Noroviruses commonly isolated in cases of acute gastroenteritis belong to two genogroups: genogroup I (GI), which
includes Norwalk virus, Desert Shield virus, and Southampton virus; and II (GII), which includes Bristol virus, Lordsdale
virus, Toronto virus, Mexico virus, Hawaii virus, and Snow Mountain virus.
Most noroviruses that infect humans belong to genogroups GI and GII. Noroviruses from genogroup II, genotype 4
(abbreviated as GII.4), account for the majority of adult outbreaks of gastroenteritis and often sweep across the globe.
Recent examples include the US95/96-US strain, associated with global outbreaks in the mid- to late-1990s;
Farmington Hills virus associated with outbreaks in Europe and the United States in 2002 and in 2004; and the Hunter
virus, which was associated with outbreaks in Europe, Japan, and Australasia. In 2006, there was another large
increase in NoV infection around the globe. Reports have shown a link between the expression of human histo-<color=#3366CC>blood</color>
<color=#3366CC>group antigens</color> (HBGAs) and the susceptibility to norovirus infection. Studies have suggested the capsid of noroviruses
may have evolved from selective pressure of human HBGAs. HBGAs are not, however, the receptor or facilitator of
norovirus infection. Co-factors such as bile salts may facilitate the infection, making it more intense when introduced
during or after the initial infection of the host tissue. Bile salts are produced by the liver in response to eating fatty
foods, and they help with the absorption of consumed <color=#3366CC>lipids</color>. It is not yet clear at what specific point in the Norovirus
replication cycle bile salts facilitate infection: penetration, uncoating, or maintaining capsid stability.
The protein MDA-5 may be the primary immune sensor that detects the presence of noroviruses in the body. Some
people have common variations of the MDA-5 gene that could make them more susceptible to norovirus infection.
Structure
Viruses in Norovirus are non-enveloped, with <color=#3366CC>icosahedral</color> geometries. Capsid diameters vary widely, from 23 to 40 <color=#3366CC>nm</color>
in diameter. The larger capsids (38–40 nm) exhibit T=3 symmetry and are composed of 180 VP1 proteins. Small
capsids (23 nm) show T=1 symmetry, and are composed of 60 VP1 proteins. The virus particles demonstrate an
amorphous surface structure when visualized using <color=#3366CC>electron microscopy</color>.
Genome
Noroviruses contain a linear, non-segmented, positive-sense <color=#3366CC>RNA</color> <color=#3366CC>genome</color> of approximately 7.5 <color=#3366CC>kilobases</color>, encoding a
large polyprotein which is cleaved into six smaller non-structural proteins (NS1/2 to NS7) by the viral 3C-like protease
(NS6), a major structural protein (VP1) of about 58~60 <color=#3366CC>kDa</color> and a minor capsid protein (VP2).
The most variable region of the viral capsid is the P2 domain, which contains antigen-presenting sites and
carbohydrate-receptor binding regions.
Evolution
Groups 1, 2, 3, and 4 last shared a common ancestor in AD 867. The group 2 and group 4 viruses last shared a
common ancestor in approximately AD 1443 (95% highest posterior density AD 1336–1542). Several estimates of the
evolution rate have been made, varying from 8.98 × 103 to 2.03 × 103 substitutions per site per year.
The estimated mutation rate (1.21 to 1.41 substitutions per site per year) in this virus is high even compared with other
RNA viruses.
In addition, a recombination hotspot exists at the ORF1-ORF2 (VP1) junction.
Replication cycle
Viral replication is cytoplasmic. Entry into the host cell is achieved by attachment to host receptors, which mediates
<color=#3366CC>endocytosis</color>. Positive-stranded RNA virus <color=#3366CC>transcription</color> is the method of replication. Translation takes place by leaky
scanning and RNA termination-reinitiation. Humans and other mammals serve as the <color=#3366CC>natural host</color>. Transmission routes
are fecal-oral and contamination.
Pathophysiology
When a person becomes infected with norovirus, the virus replicates within the <color=#3366CC>small intestine</color>. The principal symptom
is acute <color=#3366CC>gastroenteritis</color>, characterized by nausea, forceful vomiting, watery <color=#3366CC>diarrhea</color>, and abdominal pain, that develops
12 to 48 hours after exposure and lasts for 24–72 hours. Sometimes there is loss of taste, general lethargy, weakness,
muscle aches, <color=#3366CC>headache</color>, and <color=#3366CC>fever</color>. The disease is usually self-limiting.
Severe illness is rare; although people are frequently treated at the emergency ward, they are rarely admitted to the
hospital. The number of deaths from norovirus in the United States is estimated to be around 570–800 each year, with
most of these occurring in the very young, the elderly, and persons with weakened immune systems. Symptoms may
become life-threatening in these groups if <color=#3366CC>dehydration</color> or electrolyte imbalance is ignored or left untreated.
Diagnosis
Specific diagnosis of norovirus is routinely made by <color=#3366CC>polymerase chain reaction</color> (PCR) assays or quantitative PCR
assays, which give results within a few hours. These assays are very sensitive and can detect as few as 10 virus
particles. Tests such as ELISA that use <color=#3366CC>antibodies</color> against a mixture of norovirus strains are available commercially,
but lack specificity and sensitivity.
Prevention
After <color=#3366CC>infection</color>, <color=#3366CC>immunity</color> to the same strain of the virus – the genotype – protects against reinfection for six months to
two years. This immunity does not fully protect against infection with the other diverse genotypes of the virus.
In <color=#3366CC>Canada</color>, norovirus is a notifiable disease. In both the US and the UK it is not notifiable.
Hand washing and disinfectants
Hand washing with soap and water is an effective method for reducing the transmission of norovirus pathogens.
Alcohol rubs (62% <color=#3366CC>isopropyl alcohol</color>) may be used as an adjunct, but are less effective than hand-washing, as
norovirus lacks a <color=#3366CC>lipid</color> viral envelope. <color=#3366CC>Hand sanitizers</color> based on <color=#3366CC>alcohols</color> tend to be ineffective against noroviruses due
to their being non-enveloped, although some virus genotypes were found in in vitro tests with <color=#3366CC>ethanol</color> and <color=#3366CC>isopropyl</color>
<color=#3366CC>alcohol</color> to be more susceptible. Alcohol susceptibility patterns between different norovirus genotypes were found to
vary widely, and virolysis data for a single strain or genotype were not representative for all noroviruses. Another study
found that alcohol in combination with acid (1% <color=#3366CC>citric acid</color>, e.g. from 15% concentrated lemon juice) produced an
effective disinfectant of noroviruses.
Surfaces where norovirus particles may be present can be sanitised with a solution of 1.5% to 7.5% of household
bleach in water, or other disinfectants effective against norovirus.
Healthcare facilities
In healthcare environments, the prevention of nosocomial infections involves routine and terminal cleaning.
Nonflammable alcohol vapor in CO2 systems is used in health care environments where medical electronics would be
adversely affected by aerosolized chlorine or other caustic compounds.
In 2011, the CDC published a clinical practice guideline addressing strategies for the prevention and control of
norovirus gastroenteritis outbreaks in healthcare settings. Based on a systematic review of published scientific studies,
the guideline presents 51 specific evidence-based recommendations, which were organized into 12 categories: 1)
patient cohorting and isolation precautions, 2) hand hygiene, 3) patient transfer and ward closure, 4) food handlers in
healthcare, 5) diagnostics, 6) <color=#3366CC>personal protective equipment</color>, 7) environmental cleaning, 8) staff leave and policy, 9)
visitors, 10) education, 11) active case-finding, and 12) communication and notification. The guideline also identifies
eight high-priority recommendations and suggests several areas in need of future research.
Vaccine trials
LigoCyte announced in 2007 that it was working on a vaccine and had started phase 1 trials. The company has since
been taken over by Takeda Pharmaceutical Company. As of 2019, a bivalent (NoV GI.1/GII.4) intramuscular vaccine
had completed phase 1 trials. In 2020 the phase 2b trials were finished. The vaccine relies on using a virus-like particle
that is made of the norovirus capsid proteins to mimic the external structure of the virus. Since there is no RNA in this
particle, it is incapable of reproducing and cannot cause an infection.
Persistence
The norovirus can survive for long periods outside a human host depending on the surface and temperature conditions:
it can survive for weeks on hard and soft surfaces, and it can survive for months, maybe even years in contaminated
still water. A 2006 study found the virus remained on surfaces used for food preparation seven days after
contamination.
Detection in food
Routine protocols to detect norovirus in clams and oysters by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction are being
employed by governmental laboratories such as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the US.
Treatment
There is no specific medicine to treat people with norovirus illness. Treatments aim to avoid complications by measures
such as the management of dehydration caused by fluid loss in vomiting and diarrhea, and to mitigate symptoms using
antiemetics and antidiarrheals.
Epidemiology
Norovirus causes about 18% of all cases of acute gastroenteritis worldwide. It is relatively common in developed
countries and in low-mortality developing countries (20% and 19%, respectively) compared to high-mortality developing
countries (14%). Proportionately, it causes more illness in people in the community or in hospital outpatients (24% and
20% respectively) as compared with hospital inpatients (17%), in whom other causes are more common. Norovirus is
considered to be an extremely contagious virus, with a basic reproduction number estimated around 7.2; the estimated
R0 also ranges from 2.1 to as high as 14, based on different conditions. As few as 10 Norovirus virions are needed to
infect a person.
Age and emergence of new norovirus strains do not appear to affect the proportion of gastroenteritis attributable to
norovirus.
In the United States, the estimated annual number of norovirus cases As of 2023 was 21 million, representing a rate of
6,270 cases per 100,000 individuals.
Norovirus is a common cause of epidemics of gastroenteritis on <color=#3366CC>cruise ships</color>. The CDC, through its Vessel Sanitation
Program, records and investigates outbreaks of gastrointestinal illness – mostly caused by norovirus – on cruise ships
with both a US and foreign itinerary; there were 12 in 2015, and 10 from 1 January to 9 May 2016. An outbreak may
affect over 25% of passengers, and a smaller proportion of crew members.
Human genetics
Epidemiological studies have shown that individuals with different ABO(H) (histo-<color=#3366CC>blood group</color>) phenotypes are infected
with NoV strains in a <color=#3366CC>genotype</color>-specific manner. GII.4 includes global epidemic strains and binds to more histo-blood
group antigens than other genogroups. FUT2 fucosyltransferase transfers a fucose sugar to the end of the <color=#3366CC>ABO(H)</color>
precursor in gastrointestinal cells and <color=#3366CC>saliva glands</color>. The ABH-antigen produced is thought to act as a receptor for
human norovirus: A non-functional fucosyltransferase FUT2 provides high protection from the most common norovirus
strain, GII.4.
Homozygous carriers of any nonsense mutation in the FUT2 gene are called non-secretors, as no ABH-antigen is
produced. Approximately 20% of Caucasians are non-secretors due to G428A and C571T nonsense mutations in FUT2
and therefore have strong – although not absolute – protection from the norovirus GII.4. Non-secretors can still produce
ABH antigens in erythrocytes, as the precursor is formed by FUT1. Some norovirus genotypes (GI.3) can infect
non-secretors.
History
The norovirus was originally named the "Norwalk agent" after Norwalk, Ohio, in the United States, where an outbreak of
acute gastroenteritis occurred among children at Bronson Elementary School in November 1968. In 1972, electron
microscopy on stored human stool samples identified a virus, which was given the name "Norwalk virus". Numerous
outbreaks with similar symptoms have been reported since. The <color=#3366CC>cloning</color> and sequencing of the Norwalk virus genome
showed that these viruses have a genomic organization consistent with viruses belonging to the family Caliciviridae.
The name "norovirus" (Norovirus for the genus) was approved by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses
(ICTV) in 2002. In 2011, however, a press release and a newsletter were published by ICTV, which strongly
encouraged the media, national health authorities, and the scientific community to use the virus name Norwalk virus,
rather than the genus name Norovirus when referring to outbreaks of the disease. This was also a public response by
ICTV to the request from an individual in Japan to rename the Norovirus genus because of the possibility of negative
associations for people in Japan and elsewhere who have the family name "Noro". Before this position of ICTV was
made public, ICTV consulted widely with members of the Caliciviridae Study Group and carefully discussed the case.
In addition to "Norwalk agent" and "Norwalk virus", the virus has also been called "Norwalk-like virus", "small,
round-structured viruses" (SRSVs), Spencer flu, and "Snow Mountain virus". Common names of the illness caused by
noroviruses still in use include "Roskilde illness", "winter vomiting disease", "winter vomiting bug", "viral gastroenteritis",
and "acute nonbacterial gastroenteritis".
High Middle Ages
The High Middle Ages, or High Medieval Period, was the <color=#3366CC>period</color> of <color=#3366CC>European history</color> between c. 1000 and c. 1300; it
was preceded by the <color=#3366CC>Early Middle Ages</color> and followed by the <color=#3366CC>Late Middle Ages</color>, which ended c. 1500 according to
<color=#3366CC>historiographical</color> convention. Key historical trends of the High Middle Ages include the ascent of the great Italian
<color=#3366CC>city-states</color>, the rapidly increasing population of Europe, which brought about great social and political change from the
preceding era, and the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance of the 12th century</color>, including the first developments of the rural exodus and
<color=#3366CC>urbanization</color>. By 1350, the robust population increase had greatly benefited the European economy, which had reached
levels that would not be seen again in some areas until the 19th century. That trend faltered in the early 14th century,
as the result of numerous events which together comprised the <color=#3366CC>crisis of the late Middle Ages</color>—most notable among
them being the <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color>, in addition to various regional wars and economic stagnation.
The <color=#3366CC>Vikings</color> settled in the British Isles, France and elsewhere, and Norse Christian kingdoms started developing in their
Scandinavian homelands. The Magyars ceased their expansion in the 10th century, and by 1000, a Christian <color=#3366CC>Kingdom</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Hungary</color> had become a recognized state in <color=#3366CC>Central Europe</color> that was forming alliances with regional powers. With the
brief exception of the <color=#3366CC>Mongol invasions</color> in the 13th century, major nomadic incursions ceased. The powerful <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color> of the Macedonian and Komnenos dynasties gradually gave way to the resurrected Serbia and <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color> and to
a successor <color=#3366CC>crusader state</color> (1204 to 1261), who continually fought each other until the end of the Latin Empire. The
Byzantine Empire was reestablished in 1261 with the recapture of <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> from the Latins, though it was no
longer a major power and would continue to falter through the 14th century, with remnants lasting until the mid 15th
century.
In the 11th century, populations north of the <color=#3366CC>Alps</color> began a more intensive settlement, targeting "new" lands, some areas
of which had reverted to wilderness after the end of the <color=#3366CC>Western Roman Empire</color>. In what historian Charles Higounet
called the "great clearances", Europeans cleared and cultivated some of the vast forests and marshes that lay across
much of the continent. At the same time, settlers moved beyond the traditional boundaries of the <color=#3366CC>Frankish Empire</color> to
new frontiers beyond the <color=#3366CC>Elbe River</color>, which tripled the size of Germany in the process. The <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color>, which
reached the peak of its political power around then, called armies from across Europe to a series of <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color> against

the <color=#3366CC>Seljuk Turks</color>. The crusaders occupied the <color=#3366CC>Holy Land</color> and founded the <color=#3366CC>Crusader States</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>. Other wars

led to the <color=#3366CC>Northern Crusades</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Islamic civilization</color> of <color=#3366CC>Al-Andalus</color> flourished until Christian kingdoms <color=#3366CC>took much of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Iberian Peninsula</color> from <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color> control. The <color=#3366CC>Normans</color> conquered southern Italy, all part of the major population
increases and the resettlement patterns of the era.
The High Middle Ages produced many different forms of intellectual, spiritual and <color=#3366CC>artistic works</color>, including many of the

most notable <color=#3366CC>Gothic cathedrals</color>. The first universities, in <color=#3366CC>Bologna</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oxford</color>, <color=#3366CC>Paris</color>, <color=#3366CC>Salamanca</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cambridge</color> and Modena,
facilitated an encounter with <color=#3366CC>medieval Jewish</color> and <color=#3366CC>Islamic philosophy</color> and the rediscovery of the works of <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>.

<color=#3366CC>Maimonides</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ibn Sina</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ibn Rushd</color>, <color=#3366CC>Thomas Aquinas</color> and other thinkers of the period developed <color=#3366CC>Scholasticism</color>, a
combination of Judeo-Islamic and Catholic ideologies with the ancient philosophy. <color=#3366CC>Byzantine art</color> reached a peak in the
12th century.
Historical events and politics
Great Britain and Ireland
In England, the <color=#3366CC>Norman Conquest</color> of 1066 resulted in a kingdom ruled by a <color=#3366CC>Francophone</color> nobility. The <color=#3366CC>Normans</color>
invaded Ireland in 1169 and soon established themselves in most of the country, although their stronghold was the
southeast. Likewise, <color=#3366CC>Scotland</color> and <color=#3366CC>Wales</color> were subdued into <color=#3366CC>vassal states</color> at about the same time, though Scotland
later asserted its independence and Wales remained largely under the rule of independent native princes until the
death of <color=#3366CC>Llywelyn ap Gruffydd</color> in 1282. The Exchequer was founded in the 12th century under <color=#3366CC>King Henry I</color>, and the
first parliaments were convened. In 1215, after the loss of <color=#3366CC>Normandy</color>, <color=#3366CC>King John</color> signed the <color=#3366CC>Magna Carta</color> into law,
limiting the power of English monarchs.
Iberia
A key geo-strategic development in the <color=#3366CC>Iberian Peninsula</color> was the Christian conquest of <color=#3366CC>Toledo</color> in 1085. Dominated by
war, the societal structures and relations in the northern Christian kingdoms were subordinated to the demands of
omnipresent military conflict. The territorial expansion of the northern Christian kingdoms to the south brought the
creation of border societies, where military demands on knights and foot soldiers and the promotion of settlement were
prioritized over potential seigneurial income; military orders also played an important role in the borderlands in the
southern meseta. Agricultural models in areas with <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean climate</color> were generally based on biennial <color=#3366CC>crop</color>
<color=#3366CC>rotation</color>. Despite population growth, agricultural output remained relatively rigid throughout the period; between the 10th
and 13th centuries, migration southwards to exposed areas was incentivized by the possibility of enjoying privileges
and acquiring properties. Conversely, the <color=#3366CC>intensive agriculture</color>-prevalent model in Muslim-ruled lands did not require
territorial expansion. While Muslim lands enjoyed a certain demographic and financial edge, <color=#3366CC>Almoravids</color> and <color=#3366CC>Almohads</color>
from northern Africa featured volatile state structures; barring (unsuccessful) attempts to take Toledo, they did not
stand out for carrying out an expansionist policy.
Italy

Along with the existing <color=#3366CC>Republic of Venice</color>, new Italian <color=#3366CC>city-state maritime republics</color> like <color=#3366CC>Genoa</color> and <color=#3366CC>Pisa</color> (from c. 1000),
and <color=#3366CC>Florence</color> (from 1115), thrived on expanding trade, led a commercial revolution, and made Italy the most productive
region of Europe in the Middle Ages. <color=#3366CC>Pope Alexander III</color> (r. 1159–1181) strongly backed the <color=#3366CC>1167 alliance of these</color>
<color=#3366CC>northern Italian cities</color>, which defeated the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color> at the Battle of Legnano (1176) and won their effective
independence from the Empire in the Peace of Constance (1183). In 1256, <color=#3366CC>Bologna</color>’s Liber Paradisus purchased the
freedom of nearly 6,000 serfs, the first abolition of serfdom in Europe.
In 1130, <color=#3366CC>Norman conquests in southern Italy</color>, including the island of <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color> and the southern third of the <color=#3366CC>Italian Peninsula</color>
(including Benevento), were united as the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Sicily</color>. Subsequently joined to the Holy Roman Empire, it had its
moment of maximum splendor with the emperor <color=#3366CC>Frederick II</color>.
Scandinavia
From the mid-10th to the mid-11th centuries, the Scandinavian kingdoms were unified and Christianized, resulting in an
end of <color=#3366CC>Viking</color> raids, and greater involvement in European politics. King <color=#3366CC>Cnut</color> of Denmark ruled over both England and
Norway. After Cnut's death in 1035, England and Norway were both lost, and with the defeat of Valdemar II in 1227,
Danish predominance in the region came to an end. Meanwhile, Norway extended its Atlantic possessions, ranging
from <color=#3366CC>Greenland</color> to the <color=#3366CC>Isle of Man</color>, while Sweden, under Birger Jarl, built up a power-base in the <color=#3366CC>Baltic Sea</color>. However,
the Norwegian influence started to decline already in the same period, marked by the Treaty of Perth of 1266. Also, civil
wars raged in Norway between 1130 and 1240.
France and Germany
By the time of the High Middle Ages, the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Empire</color> had been divided and replaced by separate successor
kingdoms called France and Germany, although not with their modern boundaries. France pushed to the west. The
<color=#3366CC>Angevin Empire</color> controlled much of France in the 12th century and early 13th century until the French retook much of
their previous territory.
Germany
By the time of the High Middle Ages, the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian Empire</color> had been divided and replaced by separate successor
kingdoms called France and Germany, although not with their modern boundaries. Germany was significantly more
eastern. Germany was under the banner of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color>, which reached its high-water mark of unity and
political power under <color=#3366CC>Kaiser Frederick Barbarossa</color>.
Georgia
During the successful reign of King <color=#3366CC>David IV of Georgia</color> (1089–1125), the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Georgia</color> grew in strength and
expelled the <color=#3366CC>Seljuk Empire</color> from its lands. David's decisive victory in the Battle of Didgori (1121) against the Seljuk
Turks, as a result of which Georgia recaptured its lost capital <color=#3366CC>Tbilisi</color>, marked the beginning of the Georgian Golden Age.
David's granddaughter <color=#3366CC>Queen Tamar</color> continued the upward rise, successfully neutralizing internal opposition and
embarking on an energetic foreign policy aided by further decline of the hostile <color=#3366CC>Seljuk Turks</color>. Relying on a powerful
military elite, Tamar was able to build on the successes of her predecessors to consolidate an empire which dominated
vast lands spanning from present-day southern <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> on the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color> to the <color=#3366CC>Caspian Sea</color>. Georgia remained a
leading regional power until its collapse under the <color=#3366CC>Mongol</color> attacks within two decades after Tamar's death.
Hungary
In the High Middle Ages, Hungary became one of the most powerful medieval states in Europe. The Christian <color=#3366CC>Kingdom</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Hungary</color> was established in 1000 under King <color=#3366CC>Saint Stephen I of Hungary</color>, and ruled by the Árpád dynasty for the
following centuries. King Saint Ladislaus completed the work of King <color=#3366CC>Saint Stephen</color>. He consolidated the Hungarian
state power and strengthened the influence of <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>. His charismatic personality, strategic leadership and military
talents resulted the termination of internal power struggles and foreign military threats. The Kingdom of Hungary

expanded to the <color=#3366CC>Adriatic</color> coast and entered a <color=#3366CC>personal union</color> with <color=#3366CC>Croatia</color> in 1102, by establish other <color=#3366CC>vassal states</color>,
Hungary became a small empire that extended its control over the Southeast Europe and the <color=#3366CC>Carpathian</color> region. The
Hungarian royal Árpád dynasty gave the world the most saints and blessed from a single family.
Lithuania
During the High Middle Ages Lithuania emerged as a Duchy of Lithuania in the early 13th century, then briefly
becoming the Kingdom of Lithuania from 1251 to 1263. After the assassination of its first Christian king <color=#3366CC>Mindaugas</color>
Lithuania was known as <color=#3366CC>Grand Duchy of Lithuania</color>. Unconquered during the Lithuanian Crusade, Lithuania itself rapidly
expanded to the East due to conquests and became one of the largest states in Europe.
Poland
In the mid-10th century Poland emerged as a duchy after <color=#3366CC>Mieszko I</color>, the ruler of the Polans, conquered the surrounding
Lechitic tribes in the region. Then in 1025 under the rule of <color=#3366CC>Bolesław I the Brave</color>, Poland became a kingdom.
Southeast Europe
The High Middle Ages saw the height and decline of the Slavic state of <color=#3366CC>Kievan Rus'</color> and emergence of <color=#3366CC>Cumania</color>. Later,
the <color=#3366CC>Mongol invasion</color> in the 13th century had a great impact on the east of <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, as many countries of the region were
invaded, pillaged, conquered or vassalized.
During the first half of this period (c. 1025—1185), the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color> dominated Southeast Europe, and under the
Komnenian emperors there was a revival of prosperity and urbanization; however, their domination of Southeast
Europe was coming to an end with a successful Vlach-Bulgarian rebellion in 1185, and henceforth the region was
divided between the Byzantines in Greece, some parts of Macedonia, and <color=#3366CC>Thrace</color>, the Bulgarians in Moesia and most
of Thrace and Macedonia, and the Serbs to the northwest. Eastern and Western churches had formally split in the 11th
century, and despite occasional periods of co-operation during the 12th century, in 1204 the <color=#3366CC>Fourth Crusade</color>
treacherously captured <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color>. This severely damaged the Byzantines, and their power was ultimately
weakened by the <color=#3366CC>Seljuks</color> and the rising <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> in the 14–15th century. The power of the <color=#3366CC>Latin Empire</color>,
however, was short-lived after the Crusader army was routed by Bulgarian Emperor Kaloyan in the Battle of Adrianople
Climate and agriculture
The Medieval Warm Period, the period from the 10th century to about the 14th century in Europe, was a relatively
warm and gentle interval ended by the generally colder <color=#3366CC>Little Ice Age</color> which would continue until the middle of the 19th
century. Farmers grew <color=#3366CC>wheat</color> well north into Scandinavia, and <color=#3366CC>wine</color> grapes in northern England, although the maximum
expansion of vineyards appeared to occur within the Little Ice Age period. During this time, a high demand for wine and
steady volume of <color=#3366CC>alcohol consumption</color> inspired a viticulture revolution of progress. The relative protection from <color=#3366CC>famine</color>
during this time allowed Europe's population to increase, despite the famine in 1315 that killed 1.5 million people. This
increased population contributed to the founding of new towns and an increase in industrial and economic activity
during the period. They also established trade and a comprehensive production of alcohol. Food production also
increased during this time as new ways of farming were introduced, including the use of a heavier plow, horses instead
of oxen, and a three-field system that allowed the cultivation of a greater variety of crops than the earlier two-field
system—notably <color=#3366CC>legumes</color>, the growth of which prevented the depletion of important nitrogen from the soil.
The rise of chivalry
During the High Middle Ages, the idea of a Christian warrior started to change as Christianity grew more prominent in
medieval Europe. The <color=#3366CC>Codes of Chivalry</color> promoted the ideal knight to be selfless, faithful, and fierce against those who
threaten the weak. Household heavy cavalry (<color=#3366CC>knights</color>) became common in the 11th century across Europe, and
tournaments were invented. Tournaments allowed knights to establish their family name while being able to gather vast
wealth and renown through victories. In the 12th century, the Cluny monks promoted ethical warfare and inspired the
formation of orders of chivalry, such as the <color=#3366CC>Templar Knights</color>. Inherited titles of nobility were established during this
period. In 13th-century Germany, knighthood became another <color=#3366CC>inheritable</color> title, although one of the less prestigious, and
the trend spread to other countries.
Religion
Christian Church
The second half of the 11th century saw a rapid and radical transformation in the character of the Rome-based Latin
Church. In 1046 the Holy Roman Emperor <color=#3366CC>Henry III</color> (r. 1046–1056) deposed Pope Gregory VI (r. 1045–1046) — who
had purchased the papacy — along with two other claimants, beginning the process of freeing the papacy from the
<color=#3366CC>control of the local Roman nobility</color>. <color=#3366CC>Pope Leo IX</color> (r. 1049–1054), a German, recruited an international circle of radical
reformers who helped him create an "itinerant papacy" that moved from city to city to hold church councils, consecrate
cathedrals, and negotiate with secular rulers. After centuries of growing rivalry, Leo's dynamic papacy also precipitated
the <color=#3366CC>East–West Schism</color> (also "Great Schism") that split the Latin Church from the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox Church</color> of the
Byzantine Empire in 1054. One of Leo's reformist successors, Pope Nicholas II (r. 1059–1061), and his influential
advisor Cardinal <color=#3366CC>Hildebrand of Sovana</color>, issued the papal bull In nomine Domini (1059), which stripped the Holy Roman
Emperor of his traditional role in appointing popes and established the <color=#3366CC>College of Cardinals</color> as the sole electors. After
Cardinal Hildebrand was himself elected <color=#3366CC>Pope Gregory VII</color> (r. 1073–1085), he worked both to improve the moral
integrity and independence of Church clergy (including making celibacy mandatory) and to establish the total freedom
of the Church from secular interference ("libertas ecclesiae"). By challenging the Holy Roman Emperor <color=#3366CC>Henry IV</color>'s (r.
1084–1105) right to appoint church officials, Gregory began the <color=#3366CC>Investiture Controversy</color>, a struggle for supremacy
between the Church and the secular monarchies of Europe.
Crusades
In 1095 the Byzantine emperor <color=#3366CC>Alexios I Komnenos</color> requested military support in his <color=#3366CC>Empire's conflict with the Seljuk</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color>. In response, <color=#3366CC>Pope Urban II</color> (r. 1088-1099) spread a <color=#3366CC>message of holy war</color> across Europe. The ensuing
<color=#3366CC>Crusades</color> led to the foundation of <color=#3366CC>small Catholic states</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>, which lasted for two centuries until their final
outpost, Acre, <color=#3366CC>fell</color> to the <color=#3366CC>Mamluk Sultanate</color> in 1291.
Military orders
In the context of the crusades, monastic military orders were founded that would become the template for the late
medieval chivalric orders.
The <color=#3366CC>Knights Templar</color> were a Christian military order founded after the <color=#3366CC>First Crusade</color> to help protect Christian pilgrims
from hostile locals and highway bandits. The order was deeply involved in banking, and in 1307 <color=#3366CC>Philip the Fair</color>
(Philippine le Bel) had the entire order arrested in France and dismantled on charges of alleged heresy.
The <color=#3366CC>Knights Hospitaller</color> were originally a <color=#3366CC>Christian</color> organization founded in <color=#3366CC>Jerusalem</color> in 1080 to provide care for poor,
sick, or injured <color=#3366CC>pilgrims</color> to the <color=#3366CC>Holy Land</color>. After Jerusalem was taken in the First Crusade, it became a religious/military
order that was charged with the care and defence of the <color=#3366CC>Crusader states</color>. After the Holy Lands were eventually taken
by Muslim forces, it moved its operations to <color=#3366CC>Rhodes</color>, and later <color=#3366CC>Malta</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Teutonic Knights</color> were a German religious order formed in 1190, in the city of Acre, to aid Christian pilgrims on
their way to the Holy Lands and to operate hospitals for the sick and injured in <color=#3366CC>Outremer</color>. After Muslim forces captured
the Holy Lands, the order moved to <color=#3366CC>Transylvania</color> in 1211 and later, after being expelled, invaded pagan <color=#3366CC>Prussia</color> with
the intention of Christianizing the Baltic region. Yet, both before and after the Order's main pagan opponent, <color=#3366CC>Lithuania</color>,
converted to Christianity, the Order had already attacked other Christian nations such as <color=#3366CC>Novgorod</color> and Poland. The
Teutonic Knights' power hold, which became considerable, was broken in 1410, at the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Grunwald</color>, where the
Order suffered a devastating defeat against a joint Polish-Lithuanian army. After Grunwald, the Order declined in power
until 1809 when it was officially dissolved. There were ten crusades in total.
Golden age of monasticism
• The late 11th century/early-mid 12th century was the height of the golden age of <color=#3366CC>Christian monasticism</color> (8th-12th
centuries).
• <color=#3366CC>Benedictine Order</color> – black-robed monks
• Cistercian Order – white-robed monks
• <color=#3366CC>Bernard of Clairvaux</color>
Mendicant orders
• The 13th century saw the rise of the Mendicant orders such as the:
• <color=#3366CC>Franciscans</color> (Friars Minor, commonly known as the Grey Friars), founded 1209
• Carmelites (Hermits of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Carmel, commonly known as the White Friars), founded
• <color=#3366CC>Dominicans</color> (Order of Preachers, commonly called the Black Friars), founded 1215
• Augustinians (Hermits of St. Augustine, commonly called the Austin Friars), founded 1256
Heretical movements
Christian <color=#3366CC>heresies</color> existed in Europe before the 11th century but only in small numbers and of local character: in most
cases, a rogue priest, or a village returning to pagan traditions. However, beginning in the 11th century,
mass-movement heresies appeared. The roots of this can be partially sought in the rise of urban cities, free merchants,
and a new money-based economy. The rural values of monasticism held little appeal to urban people who began to
form sects more in tune with urban culture. The first large-scale heretical movements in Western Europe originated in
the newly urbanized areas such as southern France and northern Italy and were probably influenced by the Bogomils
and other dualist movements. These heresies were on a scale the Catholic Church had never seen before and as such
the response was one of elimination for some (such as the <color=#3366CC>Cathars</color>). Some Catholic monastic leaders, such as <color=#3366CC>Francis</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Assisi</color>, the founder of the <color=#3366CC>Franciscans</color>, had to be recognized directly by the Pope so as not to be confused with
actual heretical movements such as the Waldensians.
Cathars
Catharism was a movement with <color=#3366CC>Gnostic</color> elements that originated around the middle of the 10th century, branded by
the contemporary <color=#3366CC>Roman Catholic Church</color> as <color=#3366CC>heretical</color>. It existed throughout much of <color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color>, but its
origination was in <color=#3366CC>Languedoc</color> and surrounding areas in southern France.
The name Cathar stems from <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> katharos, "pure". One of the first recorded uses is Eckbert von Schönau who wrote
on heretics from Cologne in 1181: "Hos nostra Germania catharos appellat." ([In] our Germany [one] calls these
[people] "Cathars".)
The Cathars are also called Albigensians. This name originates from the end of the 12th century, and was used by the
chronicler Geoffroy du Breuil of Vigeois in 1181. The name refers to the southern town of Albi (the ancient Albiga). The
designation is hardly exact, for the centre was at <color=#3366CC>Toulouse</color> and in the neighbouring districts.
The <color=#3366CC>Albigensians</color> were strong in southern France, northern Italy, and the southwestern <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color>.
The Bogomils were strong in the Southeastern Europe, and became the official religion supported by the Bosnian
kings.
• Dualists believed that historical events were the result of struggle between a good (spiritual) force and an evil
(material) force and that the world was of the evil force, though it could be controlled or defeated through
<color=#3366CC>asceticism</color> and good works.
• <color=#3366CC>Albigensian Crusade</color>, <color=#3366CC>Simon de Montfort</color>, Montségur, Château de Quéribus
Waldensians
Peter Waldo of <color=#3366CC>Lyon</color> was a wealthy merchant who gave up his riches around 1175 after a religious experience and
became a preacher. He founded the Waldensians which became a Christian sect believing that all religious practices
should have strictly scriptural bases. Waldo was denied the right to preach his sermons by the Third Lateran Council in
1179, which he did not obey and continued to speak freely until he was excommunicated in 1184. Waldo was critical of
the Christian clergy saying they did not live according to the word. He rejected the practice of selling indulgences
(simony), as well as the common saint cult practices of the day.
Waldensians are considered a forerunner to the <color=#3366CC>Protestant Reformation</color>, and they melted into <color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color> with the
outbreak of the Reformation and became a part of the wider <color=#3366CC>Reformed tradition</color> after the views of <color=#3366CC>John Calvin</color> and his
theological successors in <color=#3366CC>Geneva</color> proved very similar to their own theological thought. Waldensian churches still exist,
located on several continents.
Trade and commerce
In Northern Europe, the <color=#3366CC>Hanseatic League</color>, a federation of free cities to advance trade by sea, was founded in the 12th
century, with the foundation of the city of <color=#3366CC>Lübeck</color>, which would later dominate the League, in 1158–1159. Many

northern cities of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color> became Hanseatic cities, including <color=#3366CC>Amsterdam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cologne</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bremen</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hanover</color>
and Berlin. Hanseatic cities outside the Holy Roman Empire were, for instance, <color=#3366CC>Bruges</color> and the Polish city of <color=#3366CC>Gdańsk</color>
(Danzig), as well as Königsberg, capital of the monastic state of the Teutonic Knights. In <color=#3366CC>Bergen</color>, Norway and <color=#3366CC>Veliky</color>
<color=#3366CC>Novgorod</color>, Russia the league had factories and middlemen. In this period the Germans started colonising Europe
beyond the Empire, into <color=#3366CC>Prussia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Silesia</color>.
In the late 13th century, a <color=#3366CC>Venetian</color> explorer named <color=#3366CC>Marco Polo</color> became one of the first Europeans to travel the <color=#3366CC>Silk</color>
<color=#3366CC>Road</color> to China. Westerners became more aware of the Far East when Polo documented his travels in <color=#3366CC>Il Milione</color>. He
was followed by numerous Christian missionaries to the East, such as <color=#3366CC>William of Rubruck</color>, <color=#3366CC>Giovanni da Pian del</color>
<color=#3366CC>Carpine</color>, André de Longjumeau, Odoric of Pordenone, Giovanni de' Marignolli, Giovanni di Monte Corvino, and other
travellers such as Niccolò de' Conti.
Natural philosophy
The oldest university currently in continuous operation in the world appeared in the 11th century in Italy (the <color=#3366CC>University</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Bologna</color>) and two more were established in the 12th century in France (the <color=#3366CC>University of Paris</color>) and England (the
<color=#3366CC>University of Oxford</color>). These new institutions were a foundation for many of Europe's future achievements, especially in
science. The increased contact with the Islamic world in <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> and Sicily during the <color=#3366CC>Reconquista</color>, and the Byzantine
world and Muslim <color=#3366CC>Levant</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Crusades</color>, allowed Europeans access to scientific Arabic and Greek texts,

including the works of <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alhazen</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Averroes</color>. The European universities aided materially in the <color=#3366CC>translation</color>
<color=#3366CC>and propagation of these texts</color>, catalyzing the rise of <color=#3366CC>scholasticism</color> during <color=#3366CC>Renaissance of the 12th century</color>.
At the beginning of the 13th century there were reasonably accurate Latin translations of the main works of almost all
the intellectually crucial ancient authors, The <color=#3366CC>natural philosophy</color> contained in these texts was assimilated by notable

<color=#3366CC>scholastics</color> such as <color=#3366CC>Robert Grosseteste</color>, <color=#3366CC>Roger Bacon</color>, <color=#3366CC>Albertus Magnus</color> and <color=#3366CC>Duns Scotus</color>. Precursors of the modern
<color=#3366CC>scientific method</color> can be seen already in Grosseteste's emphasis on mathematics as a way to understand nature, and
in the empirical approach admired by Bacon, particularly in his Opus Majus.
The new <color=#3366CC>Christian</color> method of learning was influenced by <color=#3366CC>Anselm of Canterbury</color> (1033–1109) from the rediscovery of
the works of <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>, at first indirectly through Medieval Jewish and Muslim Philosophy (<color=#3366CC>Maimonides</color>, <color=#3366CC>Avicenna</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Averroes</color>) and then through <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>'s own works brought back from <color=#3366CC>Byzantine</color> and Muslim libraries; and those whom

he influenced, most notably <color=#3366CC>Albertus Magnus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bonaventure</color> and <color=#3366CC>Abélard</color>. Many scholastics believed in <color=#3366CC>empiricism</color> and
supporting Roman Catholic doctrines through secular study, reason, and logic. They opposed <color=#3366CC>Christian mysticism</color>, and
the Platonist-Augustinian belief that the <color=#3366CC>mind</color> is an immaterial substance. The most famous of the <color=#3366CC>scholastics</color> was
<color=#3366CC>Thomas Aquinas</color> (later declared a "Doctor of the Church"), who led the move away from the <color=#3366CC>Platonic</color> and <color=#3366CC>Augustinian</color>
and towards Aristotelianism. Aquinas developed a <color=#3366CC>philosophy of mind</color> by writing that the <color=#3366CC>mind</color> was at birth a tabula rasa
("blank slate") that was given the ability to think and recognize forms or ideas through a divine spark. Other notable
scholastics included <color=#3366CC>Muhammad Averroes</color>, Roscelin, Abélard, Peter Lombard, and Francisco Suárez. One of the main
questions during this time was the <color=#3366CC>problem of universals</color>. Prominent opponents of various aspects of the scholastic
mainstream included <color=#3366CC>Duns Scotus</color>, <color=#3366CC>William of Ockham</color>, <color=#3366CC>Peter Damian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bernard of Clairvaux</color>, and the Victorines.
Technology
During the 12th and 13th century in Europe there was a radical change in the rate of new inventions, innovations in the
ways of managing traditional means of production, and economic growth. In less than a century there were more
inventions developed and applied usefully than in the previous thousand years of human history all over the globe. The

period saw major <color=#3366CC>technological</color> advances, including the adoption or invention of <color=#3366CC>windmills</color>, <color=#3366CC>watermills</color>, <color=#3366CC>printing</color> (though

not yet with movable type), <color=#3366CC>gunpowder</color>, the <color=#3366CC>astrolabe</color>, <color=#3366CC>glasses</color>, <color=#3366CC>scissors</color> of the modern shape, a better <color=#3366CC>clock</color>, and
greatly improved ships. The latter two advances made possible the dawn of the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color>. These inventions
were influenced by foreign culture and society.
Alfred W. Crosby described some of this technological revolution in The Measure of Reality: Quantification in Western
Europe, 1250-1600 and other major historians of technology have also noted it.
• The earliest written record of a <color=#3366CC>windmill</color> is from <color=#3366CC>Yorkshire</color>, England, dated 1185.
• <color=#3366CC>Paper</color> manufacture began in Italy around 1270.
• The <color=#3366CC>spinning wheel</color> was brought to Europe (probably from India) in the 13th century.
• The <color=#3366CC>magnetic compass</color> aided navigation, first reaching Europe some time in the late 12th century.
• Eye <color=#3366CC>glasses</color> were invented in Italy in the late 1280s.
• The <color=#3366CC>astrolabe</color> returned to Europe via Islamic Spain.
• <color=#3366CC>Fibonacci</color> introduces <color=#3366CC>Hindu-Arabic numerals</color> to Europe with his book Liber Abaci in 1202.
• The West's oldest known depiction of a stern-mounted <color=#3366CC>rudder</color> can be found on church carvings dating to around
Arts
Visual arts
Art in the High Middle Ages includes these important movements:
• <color=#3366CC>Anglo-Saxon art</color> was influential on the British Isles until the Norman Invasion of 1066
• <color=#3366CC>Romanesque art</color> continued traditions from the Classical world (not to be confused with <color=#3366CC>Romanesque architecture</color>)
• <color=#3366CC>Gothic art</color> developed a distinct Germanic flavor (not to be confused with <color=#3366CC>Gothic architecture</color>).
• Indo-Islamic architecture begins when <color=#3366CC>Muhammad of Ghor</color> made <color=#3366CC>Delhi</color> a Muslim capital
• <color=#3366CC>Byzantine art</color> continued earlier Byzantine traditions, influencing much of Eastern Europe.
• <color=#3366CC>Illuminated manuscripts</color> gained prominence both in the Catholic and Orthodox churches
Architecture
Gothic architecture superseded the <color=#3366CC>Romanesque</color> style by combining <color=#3366CC>flying buttresses</color>, gothic (or pointed) <color=#3366CC>arches</color> and
ribbed vaults. It was influenced by the spiritual background of the time, being religious in essence: thin horizontal lines
and grates made the building strive towards the sky. Architecture was made to appear light and weightless, as opposed
to the dark and bulky forms of the previous <color=#3366CC>Romanesque style</color>. It was commonly thought that light was an expression of
God; therefore, architectural techniques were adapted and developed to build churches that reflected this teaching.
Colorful <color=#3366CC>glass windows</color> enhanced the spirit of lightness. As color was much rarer at medieval times than today, it can
be assumed that these virtuoso works of art had an awe-inspiring impact on the common man from the street.
High-rising intricate ribbed, and later fan vaultings demonstrated movement toward heaven. Veneration of God was
also expressed by the relatively large size of these buildings. A gothic cathedral therefore not only invited the visitors to
elevate themselves spiritually, it was also meant to demonstrate the greatness of God. The <color=#3366CC>floor plan</color> of a gothic
cathedral corresponded to the rules of scholasticism: According to <color=#3366CC>Erwin Panofsky</color>'s Gothic Architecture and
Scholasticism, the plan was divided into sections and uniform subsections. These characteristics are exhibited by the
most famous sacral building of the time: <color=#3366CC>Notre Dame de Paris</color>.
Literature
A variety of cultures influenced the literature of the High Middle Ages, one of the strongest among them being
Christianity. The connection to Christianity was greatest in <color=#3366CC>Latin literature</color>, which influenced the vernacular languages in
the literary cycle of the Matter of Rome. Other <color=#3366CC>literary</color> cycles, or interrelated groups of stories, included the Matter of
France (stories about <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color> and his court), the Acritic songs dealing with the chivalry of <color=#3366CC>Byzantium's</color>
frontiersmen, and perhaps the best known cycle, the <color=#3366CC>Matter of Britain</color>, which featured tales about <color=#3366CC>King Arthur</color>, his court,
and related stories from <color=#3366CC>Brittany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cornwall</color>, <color=#3366CC>Wales</color> and Ireland. An anonymous German poet tried to bring the Germanic
myths from the <color=#3366CC>Migration Period</color> to the level of the French and British epics, producing the <color=#3366CC>Nibelungenlied</color>. There was
also a quantity of poetry and historical writings which were written during this period, such as <color=#3366CC>Historia Regum</color>
<color=#3366CC>Britanniae</color> by <color=#3366CC>Geoffrey of Monmouth</color>.
Despite political decline during the late 12th and much of the 13th centuries, the Byzantine scholarly tradition remained
particularly fruitful over the time period. One of the most prominent philosophers of the 11th century, <color=#3366CC>Michael Psellos</color>,
reinvigorated <color=#3366CC>Neoplatonism</color> on Christian foundations and bolstered the study of <color=#3366CC>ancient philosophical texts</color>, along with
contributing to history, grammar, and rhetorics. His pupil and successor at the head of Philosophy at the University of
Constantinople Ioannes Italos continued the Platonic line in Byzantine thought and was criticized by the Church for
holding opinions it considered heretical, such as the doctrine of <color=#3366CC>transmigration</color>. Two Orthodox theologians important in
the dialogue between the eastern and western churches were Nikephoros Blemmydes and Maximus Planudes.
Byzantine historical tradition also flourished with the works of the brothers Niketas and Michael Choniates in the
beginning of the 13th century and George Akropolites a generation later. Dating from 12th century Byzantine Empire is
also Timarion, an Orthodox Christian anticipation of <color=#3366CC>Divine Comedy</color>. Around the same time the so-called Byzantine
novel rose in popularity with its synthesis of ancient pagan and contemporaneous Christian themes.
At the same time southern France gave birth to Occitan literature, which is best known for <color=#3366CC>troubadours</color> who sang of
courtly love. It included elements from Latin literature and Arab-influenced Spain and North Africa. Later its influence
spread to several cultures in Western Europe, notably in Portugal and the Minnesänger in Germany. Provençal
literature also reached Sicily and Northern Italy laying the foundation of the "sweet new style" of <color=#3366CC>Dante</color> and later
<color=#3366CC>Petrarca</color>. Indeed, the most important poem of the <color=#3366CC>Late Middle Ages</color>, the allegorical <color=#3366CC>Divine Comedy</color>, is to a large degree
a product of both the <color=#3366CC>theology of Thomas Aquinas</color> and the largely secular Occitan literature.
Music
The surviving music of the High Middle Ages is primarily religious in nature, since <color=#3366CC>music notation</color> developed in religious
institutions, and the application of notation to secular music was a later development. Early in the period, <color=#3366CC>Gregorian</color>
<color=#3366CC>chant</color> was the dominant form of church music; other forms, beginning with organum, and later including clausulae,
conductus, and the motet, developed using the chant as source material.
During the 11th century, <color=#3366CC>Guido of Arezzo</color> was one of the first to develop musical notation, which made it easier for
singers to remember Gregorian chants.
It was during the 12th and 13th centuries that Gregorian plainchant gave birth to polyphony, which appeared in the
works of French Notre Dame School (<color=#3366CC>Léonin</color> and <color=#3366CC>Pérotin</color>). Later it evolved into the ars nova (Philippe de Vitry,
<color=#3366CC>Guillaume de Machaut</color>) and the musical genres of late Middle Ages. An important composer during the 12th century
was the <color=#3366CC>nun</color> <color=#3366CC>Hildegard of Bingen</color>.
The most significant secular movement was that of the <color=#3366CC>troubadours</color>, who arose in <color=#3366CC>Occitania</color> (Southern France) in the
late 11th century. The troubadours were often itinerant, came from all classes of society, and wrote songs on a variety
of topics, though with a particular focus on courtly love. Their style went on to influence the trouvères of northern
France, the minnesingers of Germany, and the composers of secular music of the Trecento in northern Italy.
Theatre
Economic and political changes in the High Middle Ages led to the formation of <color=#3366CC>guilds</color> and the growth of towns, and this
would lead to significant changes for theatre starting in this time and continuing into the <color=#3366CC>Late Middle Ages</color>. Trade guilds
began to perform plays, usually religiously based, and often dealing with a biblical story that referenced their
profession. For instance, a baker's guild would perform a reenactment of the <color=#3366CC>Last Supper</color>. In the <color=#3366CC>British Isles</color>, plays
were produced in some 127 different towns during the Middle Ages. These vernacular <color=#3366CC>Mystery plays</color> were written in
cycles of a large number of plays: York (48 plays), Chester (24), Wakefield (32) and Unknown (42). A larger number of
plays survive from France and Germany in this period and some type of religious dramas were performed in nearly

every European country in the Late Middle Ages. Many of these plays contained <color=#3366CC>comedy</color>, <color=#3366CC>devils</color>, <color=#3366CC>villains</color> and <color=#3366CC>clowns</color>.
There were also a number of secular performances staged in the Middle Ages, the earliest of which is The Play of the
Greenwood by Adam de la Halle in 1276. It contains satirical scenes and <color=#3366CC>folk</color> material such as <color=#3366CC>faeries</color> and other
supernatural occurrences. <color=#3366CC>Farces</color> also rose dramatically in popularity after the 13th century. The majority of these plays
come from France and Germany and are similar in tone and form, emphasizing sex and bodily excretions.

Miocene
The Miocene is the first <color=#3366CC>geological epoch</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Neogene</color> Period and extends from about (Ma). The Miocene was
named by Scottish geologist <color=#3366CC>Charles Lyell</color> and comes from <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greek</color> (meíōn), lit. 'less', and (kainós), lit. 'new' or
'recent', and thus means "less recent", because it has 18% fewer modern marine invertebrates than the <color=#3366CC>Pliocene</color> has.
The Miocene followed the <color=#3366CC>Oligocene</color> and preceded the Pliocene.
As Earth went from the Oligocene through the Miocene and into the Pliocene, the climate slowly cooled towards a
series of <color=#3366CC>ice ages</color>. The Miocene boundaries are not marked by distinct global events but by regionally defined
transitions from the warmer Oligocene to the cooler Pliocene Epoch.
During the Early Miocene, Afro-Arabia collided with Eurasia, severing the connection between the Mediterranean and
Indian Oceans and enabling the interchange of fauna between the continents, including the dispersal of <color=#3366CC>proboscideans</color>
and <color=#3366CC>hominoids</color> into Eurasia. During the late Miocene, the connections between the Atlantic and Mediterranean closed,
causing the Mediterranean Sea to almost completely evaporate. This event is referred to as the "Messinian salinity
crisis". Then, at the Miocene–Pliocene boundary, the <color=#3366CC>Strait of Gibraltar</color> opened, and the Mediterranean refilled. That
event is referred to as the "Zanclean flood".
Also during the early Miocene (specifically the Aquitanian and Burdigalian Stages), the <color=#3366CC>apes</color> first evolved, began
diversifying, and became widespread throughout the <color=#3366CC>Old World</color>. Around the end of this epoch, the <color=#3366CC>ancestors of humans</color>
had split away from the ancestors of the <color=#3366CC>chimpanzees</color> and had begun following their own evolutionary path during the
final Messinian Stage (7.5–5.3 Ma) of the Miocene. As in the Oligocene before it, <color=#3366CC>grasslands</color> continued to expand, and
forests to dwindle. In the seas of the Miocene, <color=#3366CC>kelp forests</color> made their first appearance and soon became one of Earth's
most productive ecosystems.
The plants and animals of the Miocene were recognizably modern. Mammals and birds were well established. <color=#3366CC>Whales</color>,
<color=#3366CC>pinnipeds</color>, and <color=#3366CC>kelp</color> spread.
The Miocene is of particular interest to geologists and palaeoclimatologists because major phases of the <color=#3366CC>geology of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Himalaya</color> occurred during that epoch, affecting <color=#3366CC>monsoonal</color> patterns in Asia, which were interlinked with glacial periods
in the northern hemisphere.
Subdivisions
The Miocene <color=#3366CC>faunal stages</color> from youngest to oldest are typically named according to the International Commission on
Stratigraphy:
Land mammal ages
Cenozoic mammal faunas are often described using biochronological or <color=#3366CC>biostratigraphic</color> systems, which arrange rock
strata or intervals of time based on distinctive fossil assemblages or the evolution of new mammal species. Apart from
Antarctica, each continent has a unique series of Cenozoic land mammal ages (LMAs) overprinted on the global
geological time scale. These different land mammal ages are listed in the following table, which shows rough
correlations to each other and the six global ages/stages of the Miocene:
Paleogeography
Continents continued to <color=#3366CC>drift</color> toward their present positions. Of the modern geologic features, only the land bridge
between <color=#3366CC>South America</color> and <color=#3366CC>North America</color> was absent, although South America was approaching the western
<color=#3366CC>subduction zone</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color>, causing both the rise of the <color=#3366CC>Andes</color> and a southward extension of the
<color=#3366CC>Meso-American</color> peninsula.
Mountain building took place in western <color=#3366CC>North America</color>, <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>, and <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>. Both continental and marine Miocene
deposits are common worldwide with marine outcrops common near modern shorelines. Well studied continental
exposures occur in the North American <color=#3366CC>Great Plains</color> and in <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>.
The global trend was towards increasing aridity caused primarily by global cooling reducing the ability of the
atmosphere to absorb moisture, particularly after 7 to 8 million years ago. Uplift of <color=#3366CC>East Africa</color> in the late Miocene was
partly responsible for the shrinking of <color=#3366CC>tropical rain forests</color> in that region, and <color=#3366CC>Australia</color> got drier as it entered a zone of
low rainfall in the Late Miocene.
Eurasia
The Indian Plate continued to collide with the <color=#3366CC>Eurasian Plate</color>, creating new <color=#3366CC>mountain ranges</color> and uplifting the <color=#3366CC>Tibetan</color>
<color=#3366CC>Plateau</color>, resulting in the <color=#3366CC>rain shadowing</color> and aridification of the Asian interior. The <color=#3366CC>Tian Shan</color> experienced significant
uplift in the Late Miocene, blocking westerlies from coming into the <color=#3366CC>Tarim Basin</color> and drying it as a result.
At the beginning of the Miocene, the northern margin of the <color=#3366CC>Arabian plate</color>, then part of the African landmass, collided
with Eurasia; as a result, the <color=#3366CC>Tethys</color> seaway continued to shrink and then disappeared as <color=#3366CC>Africa</color> collided with <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> in
the <color=#3366CC>Turkish</color>–<color=#3366CC>Arabian</color> region. The first step of this closure occurred 20 Ma, reducing water mass exchange by 90%,
while the second step occurred around 13.8 Ma, coincident with a major expansion of Antarctic glaciers. This severed
the connection between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea and formed the present land connection between
Afro-Arabia and Eurasia. The subsequent <color=#3366CC>uplift of mountains</color> in the western <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color> region and a global fall in
sea levels combined to cause a temporary drying up of the Mediterranean Sea (known as the Messinian salinity crisis)
near the end of the Miocene. The Paratethys underwent a significant transgression during the early Middle Miocene.
Around 13.8 Ma, during a global sea level drop, the Eastern Paratethys was cut off from the global ocean by the
closure of the Bârlad Strait, effectively turning it into a saltwater lake. From 13.8 to 13.36 Ma, an evaporite period
similar to the later Messinian salinity crisis in the Mediterranean ensued in the Central Paratethys, cut off from sources
of freshwater input by its separation from the Eastern Paratethys. From 13.36 to 12.65 Ma, the Central Paratethys was
characterised by open marine conditions, before the reopening of the Bârlad Strait resulted in a shift to brackish-marine
conditions in the Central Paratethys, causing the Badenian-Sarmatian Extinction Event. As a result of the Bârlad Strait's
reopening, the lake levels of the Eastern Paratethys dropped as it once again became a sea.
The Fram Strait opened during the Miocene and acted as the only throughflow for Atlantic Water into the Arctic Ocean
until the <color=#3366CC>Quaternary period</color>. Due to regional uplift of the continental shelf, this water could not move through the Barents
Seaway in the Miocene.
The modern day <color=#3366CC>Mekong Delta</color> took shape after 8 Ma. <color=#3366CC>Geochemistry</color> of the Qiongdongnan Basin in the northern <color=#3366CC>South</color>
<color=#3366CC>China Sea</color> indicates the <color=#3366CC>Pearl River</color> was a major source of sediment flux into the sea during the Early Miocene and was
a major fluvial system as in the present.
South America
During the <color=#3366CC>Oligocene</color> and Early Miocene, the coast of northern Brazil, Colombia, south-central Peru, central Chile and
large swathes of inland <color=#3366CC>Patagonia</color> were subject to a <color=#3366CC>marine transgression</color>. The transgressions in the west coast of
South America are thought to be caused by a regional phenomenon while the steadily rising central segment of the
Andes represents an exception. While there are numerous registers of Oligocene–Miocene transgressions around the
world it is doubtful that these correlate.
It is thought that the Oligocene–Miocene transgression in Patagonia could have temporarily linked the Pacific and
Atlantic Oceans, as inferred from the findings of marine invertebrate fossils of both Atlantic and Pacific affinity in La
Cascada Formation. Connection would have occurred through narrow epicontinental seaways that formed channels in
a dissected topography.
The <color=#3366CC>Antarctic Plate</color> started to <color=#3366CC>subduct</color> beneath South America 14 million years ago in the Miocene, forming the Chile
Triple Junction. At first the Antarctic Plate subducted only in the southernmost tip of Patagonia, meaning that the Chile
Triple Junction lay near the <color=#3366CC>Strait of Magellan</color>. As the southern part of <color=#3366CC>Nazca Plate</color> and the Chile Rise became
consumed by subduction the more northerly regions of the Antarctic Plate begun to subduct beneath Patagonia so that
the Chile Triple Junction advanced to the north over time. The asthenospheric window associated to the triple junction
disturbed previous patterns of <color=#3366CC>mantle convection</color> beneath Patagonia inducing an uplift of ca. 1 km that reversed the
Oligocene–Miocene transgression.
As the southern <color=#3366CC>Andes rose</color> in the Middle Miocene (14–12 million years ago) the resulting <color=#3366CC>rain shadow</color> originated the
<color=#3366CC>Patagonian Desert</color> to the east.
Australia
Far northern Australia was monsoonal during the Miocene. Although northern Australia is often believed to have been
much wetter during the Miocene, this interpretation may be an artefact of preservation bias of riparian and lacustrine
plants; this finding has itself been challenged by other papers. Western Australia, like today, was arid, particularly so
during the Middle Miocene.
Climate
Climates remained moderately warm, although the slow global cooling that eventually led to the <color=#3366CC>Pleistocene</color> glaciations
continued. Although a long-term cooling trend was well under way, there is evidence of a warm period during the
Miocene when the global climate rivalled that of the <color=#3366CC>Oligocene</color>. The climate of the Miocene has been suggested as a
good analogue for future warmer climates caused by <color=#3366CC>anthropogenic global warming</color>, with this being especially true of
the global climate during the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum (MMCO), because that was the last time CO2 levels
were comparable to projected future atmospheric CO2 levels resulting from anthropogenic <color=#3366CC>climate change</color>. The Ross
Sea margin of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS) was highly dynamic during the Early Miocene.
The Miocene began with the Early Miocene Cool Event (Mi-1) around 23 million years ago, which marked the start of
the Early Miocene Cool Interval (EMCI). This cool event occurred immediately after the Oligocene-Miocene Transition
(OMT) during a major expansion of Antarctica's ice sheets, but was not associated with a significant drop in
atmospheric CO2 levels. Both continental and oceanic thermal gradients in mid-latitudes during the Early Miocene were
very similar to those at present. Global cooling caused the East Asian Summer Monsoon (EASM) to begin to take on its
modern form during the Early Miocene. From 22.1 to 19.7 Ma, the Xining Basin experienced relative warmth and
humidity amidst a broader aridification trend.
The EMCI ended 18 million years ago, giving way to the Middle Miocene Warm Interval (MMWI), the warmest part of
which was the MMCO, which began 16 million years ago. As the world transitioned into the MMCO, CO2
concentrations varied between 300 and 500 ppm. Global annual mean surface temperature during the MMCO was
about 18.4 °C. MMCO warmth was driven by the activity of the <color=#3366CC>Columbia River Basalts</color> and enhanced by decreased
<color=#3366CC>albedo</color> from the reduction of deserts and expansion of forests. <color=#3366CC>Climate modelling</color> suggests additional, currently
unknown, factors also worked to create the warm conditions of the MMCO. The MMCO saw the expansion of the
tropical climatic zone to much larger than its current size. The July ITCZ, the zone of maximal monsoonal rainfall,
moved to the north, increasing precipitation over southern China whilst simultaneously decreasing it over Indochina
during the EASM. Topographic changes in Africa caused the Somali Jet to weaken, while South Asian Summer
Monsoon (SASM) rainfall increased. Western Australia was at this time exceptionally arid. In Antarctica, average
summer temperatures on land reached 10 °C. In the oceans, the lysocline shoaled by about 0.5 km during warm
phases that corresponded to <color=#3366CC>orbital eccentricity</color> maxima. The MMCO ended around 14 million years ago, when global
temperatures fell in the Middle Miocene Climate Transition (MMCT). Abrupt increases in <color=#3366CC>opal</color> deposition indicate this
cooling was driven by enhanced drawdown of CO2 via silicate weathering. The MMCT caused a <color=#3366CC>sea surface</color>
<color=#3366CC>temperature</color> (SST) drop of approximately 6 °C in the North Atlantic. The drop in benthic foraminiferal 18O values was
most noticeable in the waters around Antarctica, suggesting cooling was most intense there. Around this time the Mi3b
glacial event (a massive expansion of Antarctic glaciers) occurred. The East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS) markedly
